Colorado State.title: A defensive disaster: CSU gets embarrassed on Homecoming, Tyson Summers is out
Colorado State.summary:
What should have been a celebration turned into another nightmare for CSU football. A record 41,000 fans packed Canvas Stadium for Homecoming and the Rams’ first Pac-12 conference game, only to watch Oregon State roll up 650 yards without punting once in a 56-26 rout. Joel and Mike break down another historically bad defensive performance before diving into the biggest story of the weekend: Jim Mora stripping defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of play-calling duties mid-game, Summers leaving the sideline, and his subsequent dismissal from the program. Was the change overdue? And, why did Mora allow the defense to reach this point in the first place? The guys examine Summers’ surprising retention from the previous staff, Mora’s own responsibility for CSU’s three-game collapse, and whether new play-caller Kenny McClendon can use the bye week to finally make this defense remotely competent.

Former Colorado State head coach Jim McElwain joins RamNation Radio for a memorable look back at the era that produced CSU’s last 10-win season and last bowl victory. Coach Mac shares stories from taking over a struggling Rams program, why recruiting Colorado was so important, beating CU twice in three years, the unforgettable 2013 New Mexico Bowl comeback over Washington State, going toe-to-toe with No. 1 Alabama and the 2014 breakthrough that put CSU back on the national map. Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga star Kevin Pangos reportedly to join Tommy Lloyd's staff at Arizona
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga point guard Kevin Pangos announced his retirement from basketball last weekend, but it appears he’s hardly finished with the sport.

According to a report online, Pangos will join Tommy Lloyd’s staff as an Arizona assistant coach.

Pangos, 33, played four years at Gonzaga while Lloyd was an assistant on the Zags staff, becoming the WCC player of the year as a senior in 2014-15 before beginning a professional career.

Pangos played 10 seasons professionally, spending last season in Turkey, before announcing his retirement via Instagram on Saturday. He played 24 games with the NBA’s Cleveland Cavaliers in 2021-22, and was also a longtime member of the Canadian national program.

“I don’t know if any athlete finishes their career completely content. We always believe we’re capable of more. But I can 1,000% say I gave it everything I had. I never let the circumstances dictate my approach.

“We left it all out there and accomplished everything you always dreamed of. Now it’s time to do the same for the next chapter.”

Pangos appears likely to take the open UA assistant coaching spot vacated when Ken Nakagawa left to become an assistant coach with the G League’s Salt Lake Stars, SB Nation reported last Friday.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with experience, Gonzaga women appear better than ever ahead of annual Fan Fest
Gonzaga.summary:
When it comes to the Gonzaga women’s basketball team’s Fan Fest, it’s less about execution and more about embracing the moment.

More than anything, it’s the first opportunity for the Zags to wear their uniforms and step onto the court at McCarthey Athletic Center in a pseudo-competitive environment. Just because the Bulldogs aren’t playing a real opponent, playing against each other can bring out the competitive spirit.

After all, teammates don’t like to lose to teammates – whether it’s a table-top game, a 3-point shooting contest or an intrasquad scrimmage.

That alone is reason for a crowd to show up Saturday when things tip off at 2 p.m. and fans can get their first look at the 2026-27 lineup.

Junior point guard Allie Turner, who has started nearly all Gonzaga games since her arrival from St. Louis, Missouri, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

Turner hopes the Zags put forward a better showing than a year ago.

“Hopefully we’re way better than last year,” Turner said of Fan Fest. “I remember some people being like ‘(we) should have moved (Fan Fest) back a few weeks last year.’ But hopefully this year we look like a well-oiled machine out there.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier was told that Turner brought up Fan Fest and her expectation of making a better debut this year.

“It’s funny that Allie brought up Fan Fest. I don’t even remember it to be honest with you,” Fortier said.

Fortier won’t be looking at the final statistics. She doesn’t put much stock in who scores what or who has the most rebounds in a scrimmage.

“The big thing is getting them under the lights,” Fortier said. “It’s good to see where everyone is. For me it’s good for my coaches to get to coach. I sit on the side and rib everybody and take notes.”

Ten of the 13 Zags have suited up for a Fan Fest. It’ll be a new experience for freshman forward Abby Lusk, GU’s lone incoming frosh from Pocatello, Idaho; guard Emmy Roach, a junior transfer from Rider University; and guard Jocelyn Medina, a senior transfer from Denver.

A roster is usually needed for Fan Fest. Not this year. Even returning is graduate guard Ines Bettencourt, who gained a fifth year of eligibility this summer late under the new 5-in-5 eligibility format. So her former uniform number (8) had been assigned to Medina. Bettencourt’s new number is 0.

Former Mead standout Teryn Gardner, who transferred from Boise State last year and made an immediate impact coming off the bench, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

“We have basically the same team back so I think we’re all super excited for that,” Gardner said. “It’s going to be a fun time.”

Gardner said the goal for Fan Fest isn’t anything complicated.

“We want to start solidifying our plays,” she said. “We want to help the three new girls get to know everything and how we run the system and whatnot. We want to have fun but we want to make it a good scrimmage.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile will be sitting on the sideline. She’s still wearing a boot on a foot she injured during the summer. The injury is healing and doesn’t appear to be longterm, Fortier said.

Haile was selected as the West Coast Conference Sixth Woman of the Year last season.

Fortier has been cautious with Haile’s recovery.

A deep roster

It stands to figure Gonzaga will be a much more polished team this year.

But there are questions to be answered. Can GU win a championship in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12? Can it win an NCAA Tournament game and go further than any previous GU team? With all five starters back, does coach Fortier just roll out the 2025-26 starting lineup? And with five other returners who got quality playing time, how does Fortier divvy up minutes?

Lots of questions and no hurry to come up with answers.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Fortier has decided to stay away from concrete specified goals with her team this year.

“We’re not even really setting those in the same way,” Fortier said. “Our team goal is to show up every day in practice. We’re not even putting that (goals) to paper. We talk about the process a lot. I think it does them a disservice to (talk about goals). They may or may not have those in the back of their heads, but we’re not gonna verbalize those things. I believe if we show up every day and try to get better then all of the end is going to take care of itself.”

Fortier is right. There will be much conversation about potential by a number of people – right, wrong or indifferent – so the Zags would do themselves favors by veering away from those conversations.

They know, for example, they’ll have a target on their backs. With essentially the whole team back they can’t help but be picked to win the Pac-12 Conference and advance to the NCAA Tournament.

There will also be talk of the potential to be the best team ever under Fortier and best in school history. But it does the Zags no good to get caught up in those expectations.

Gonzaga is going to be good. The Zags know it. The Bulldogs will be out to stack days together. And that could get them to where they want to go.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga forward Kelly Olynyk inks contract with Italian club BC Roma
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga standout Kelly Olynyk will resume his basketball career in Europe after 13 seasons in the NBA.

The 35-year-old forward signed a contract with BC Roma in Italy’s top league, the Lega Basket Serie A (LBA), the team announced on Saturday. One of the club’s co-founders is Los Angeles Lakers All-Star Luke Doncic.

“I am very happy with this opportunity and to become part of the BC Rome project,” Olynyk said after signing. “I can’t wait to arrive in Rome, meet my new teammates, and start working together with the team. I am thrilled with this new experience.”

Olynyk spent time with eight different teams over his 13 seasons in the NBA, most recently playing a deep bench role for the San Antonio Spurs team that lost 4-1 to the New York Knicks in the NBA Finals.

The journeyman forward didn’t make an appearance in the Finals, but logged minutes in four games during San Antonio’s Western Conference Finals win over the Oklahoma City Thunder. Olynyk averaged a career-low 3.2 points and 1.8 rebounds while averaging 8.6 minutes per game last season.

“He understands basketball, can space the floor with his three-point shooting and can pass the ball,” Roma coach Alessandro Magro said. “I’m confident he can fit into our systems quickly and help us right from the start.”

After being selected by the Dallas Mavericks with the 13th overall pick of the 2013 NBA Draft, Olynyk was traded to the Boston Celtics on Draft night. He played four seasons with the Celtics, mostly as a reserve, and helped the team advance to the Eastern Conference Finals.

Olynyk spent four more seasons with the Miami Heat, reaching the NBA Finals in 2020 when Erik Spoelstra’s Heat lost in six games to LeBron James and the Los Angeles Lakers.

The former Zag also had stints with the Houston Rockets (2020-21), Detroit Pistons (2021-22), Utah Jazz (2022-24), Toronto Raptors (2023-25) and New Orleans Pelicans (2024-25) before signing with the Spurs ahead of the 2025-26 season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Davis Fogle caps highlight day with 'pretty incredible' 30-point eruption at Kraziness in the Kennel
Gonzaga.summary:
Braden Huff’s Kraziness in the Kennel scoring record wasn’t on Davis Fogle’s radar when Saturday’s intrasquad scrimmage started at McCarthey Athletic Center, nor did it look like something that would be in jeopardy when Fogle missed his first two shots from the field, leaving the sophomore scoreless through five minutes.

Then Fogle drained a 3-pointer, found his offensive rhythm and continued to pump in shots from virtually every area of the floor, blowing past Huff’s scoring record with 30 points during a 56-45 victory for the White squad.

Fogle showed glimpses of his improved outside shooting, finishing 11 of 15 from the field, 6 of 7 from the 3-point line and 2 of 2 from the free-throw line. Huff previously owned the two highest-scoring scrimmage totals, with 19 points in 2023 and 17 in 2025, but Fogle officially took the record from his teammate with a 3-pointer at the 6-minute, 37-second mark and continued to attack, scoring nine points over the final five minutes.

“Luckily he was on my team, I was a little upset (about the record),” Huff said, seated two chairs down from Fogle during a post-scrimmage press conference. “He could’ve scored at least 20, 21, barely broken it, but just had to score 30. All jokes aside, that was pretty incredible. It was a good performance and we’re excited to see that against someone other than our own guys.”

Fogle, who carved out a role in Mark Few’s rotation during the final two months of his freshman season, scored all 30 of his points during a span of 14 minutes, 12 seconds, and squeezed 11 points into one two minute-stretch.

“I had no idea what the record was, just going out there hooping,” Fogle said. “I was open, they got me open, just made the shots.”

Added Huff: “I wouldn’t have passed you the ball if I would’ve known.”

Fogle, who had an ice pack taped to his left leg when he arrived to the postgame presser, delivered many of the highlights during Saturday’s preseason showcase, and not necessarily just during the 20-minute scrimmage portion.

Earlier on, he picked up a dunk contest crown after leaping over 7-foot-1 Massamba Diop, who stood at the egde of the foul circle as Fogle dribbled into the lane and took off, barely clearing the Arizona State transfer before stuffing the ball into the basket with one hand.

“It was honestly a couple weeks ago in the gym, (SID) Barrett (Henderson) talked to me about doing the dunk contest, I was like this is what I’m going to do,” Fogle said. “Tried it once, pretty easy. (Diop) was cool with it, he trusted me.”

There were other reassuring signs on Saturday for a Gonzaga team facing a litany of eligibility questions less than a month out from the season opener against Purdue.

Harwell, one of the 11 players guaranteed to be on the team’s roster for that game, scored 17 points on 6-of-8 shooting and 4 of 5 from the field in his Kraziness debut.

“It’s been amazing, especially coaches and players, I feel like we’ve all been pushing each other,” said Harwell, a Houston transfer who considered signing with Gonzaga out of high school. “Beginning of the summer, we only had about eight players so just being able to go against each other and have full reps every day and getting back to being myself again.”

Huff, who hadn’t played in front of a full crowd at the Kennel in 268 days since dislocating his kneecap, was the scrimmage’s third double-digit scorer, totaling 11 points on 4-of-11 shooting.

The quartet of Fogle, Huff, Harwell and Diop should give the Zags a solid foundation, even if one or multiple eligibility decisions don’t go their way in the upcoming weeks or months. The outlook for a projected preseason top 10-20 team would obviously be even better if fifth-year transfers Xaivian Lee, Chauncey Wiggins and Javon Bennett, and Spanish forward Izan Almansa are cleared to suit up.

Three of those four participated in Saturday’s scrimmage, with Bennett sitting out due to a minor shoulder injury the point guard suffered earlier this week. Lee started at point guard for the White squad, scoring nine points to go with four assists, while Wiggins had eight points on two made 3’s and Almansa added seven points and seven rebounds for the Blue team.

Lee is currently eligible through a temporary restraining order in California, but Wiggins and Bennett are ineligible after the NCAA was granted a stay motion in their respective state lawsuits. Almansa, meanwhile, is still waiting on the NCAA to approve his eligibility waiver.

“The best expectation would be the NCAA just lets these guys play,” Few said. “It’s really unfortunate they’re taking this stance. Classes before all these guys have gotten five, six, seven years. Now with our new rule, the classes after them. So I’m not sure why we’re sticking to targeting this one specific group.

“But now we’ve started school everywhere and rosters are set, it’s a really, really small number that are out there in these things. Our three guys are wonderful guys, they’re good students working on their Master’s. These are the type of guys we should have in college basketball.”

French point guard Nathan De Sousa, who was recently cleared to play by the NCAA, was solid for the Navy team, tallying seven points and five assists.

Collectively, the Navy and White teams combined to finish 18 of 32 (56%) from the 3-point line during Saturday’s 20-minute scrimmage – another encouraging sign for a team that shot 33.3% last season, never making more than 14 3’s in a single game.

Gonzaga.title: Multiple Zags show promise from behind 3-point arc at Kraziness
Gonzaga.summary:
For the first time in at least a decade, Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel didn’t include a 3-point competition, so the Navy and White teams used an entertaining 20-minute scrimmage to show off their perimeter shooting.

The Zags, coming off the worst 3-point shooting season (33.3%) in program history, had no issues from distance Saturday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

White, which pulled away to win 56-45, canned 11 of 17 behind the arc, paced by sophomore wing Davis Fogle’s 6 of 7. Navy wasn’t far behind, hitting 7 of 15, led by Houston transfer Isiah Harwell’s 4 of 5 on 3s.

The annual Kraziness event served as the public’s first glimpse at the 2026-27 Zags and fans got to see 3-point accuracy that often was missing on last year’s squad.

Making snap judgements from a preseason scrimmage isn’t advisable, but it was a promising sign when five different Zags – Harwell, Fogle, Florida transfer guard Xaivian Lee, Braden Huff and Florida State transfer forward Chauncey Wiggins – connected on 3-pointers in the scrimmage’s first 6 minutes and 8 seconds.

Lee finished 3 of 6 on 3s and the 6-foot-11 Wiggins made 2 of 5.

Gonzaga head coach Mark Few witnessed improved 3-point shooting throughout summer and fall drills from a revamped roster with just two returning players, Fogle and Huff.

“We’ve shot it good,” Few said. “Actually (Dayton transfer guard) Javon (Bennett, who sat out with a shoulder injury) shoots it really good, so we missed that today. But ‘X’ (Lee) has shot it good. It was nice to see Isiah step up and make some and obviously Davis has shot it really well.”

There’s a reason for that. Fogle estimated he put 500-600 shots daily in the offseason, streamlining his form with assistant coach Stephen Gentry.

“Last year I had a pretty good season, but I knew (perimeter shooting) was going to be a big step in my game, not only for college but just for the next level,” Fogle said. “Me and coach Gentry really started from zero right when season ended. We were just (taking) form shots, mid-range shots, really trying to keep (the ball) on my right side and eliminate all the moving parts.

“That, along with me coming back in the gym at night and just repping it out every day, it just became more and more comfortable.”

Fogle actually was one of the team’s better shooters last season at 35% on 3-pointers as a freshman but understood there was room for growth.

“Literally when the season was over, we started a 21-day program totally rebuilding his shot, down to how he catches the ball,” Gentry said. “The big emphasis was it’s tight to his body, it’s right and he’s really driving the ball. He’ll hear me say all the time: ‘Tight, right and drive.’

“To his credit, he totally bought in, totally coachable. He’s got a little shooting routine he goes through every single day as his warmup. He probably knows it better than me at this point.”

The 6-6 Harwell was a five-star recruit on Gonzaga’s radar before he spent his freshman year at Houston. The Cougars didn’t get the best version of Harwell, who lost valuable development time recovering from a torn ACL as a high school senior.

“At the beginning, I was with Gentry and ‘B-Mike’ (assistant Brian Michaelson) and we had just been shooting,” said Harwell, who made 27.1% on 3s while averaging just under 14 minutes per game at Houston. “Being able to have an actual offseason where I’m not in the training room as much and just being on the court and getting everything going again was nice.”

Huff, a 33.3% 3-point shooter last season, made 2 of 3 treys. The 6-10 senior, highly productive and wildly efficient inside the arc the last three seasons, was just 2 of 8 on 2-pointers.

“I took a lot of time working on (3-point shooting),” Huff said. “I just want to first off get more up this year but also make more at a higher clip. It felt good today. I’ve got to get back to making some hooks and floaters. I missed more than I usually do.”

The season opener against Purdue is roughly a month away, but Gentry, like Few, has seen encouraging signs from Gonzaga’s primary shooting threats.

“Xaivian is a way better 3-point shooter than last year’s stats,” Gentry said. “He’s got a good stroke. Javon can really shoot it. There’s nothing we’re doing with his shot. It’s ready to go. (French guard Nathan) De Sousa can shoot it, get a little more arc on his shot. Chauncey obviously can shoot it and get it off, crazy quick. (Izan) Almansa can make open 3s.

“The unique thing is, too, these guys can make 3s off the bounce, which is really important in attacking switching and respecting guys in ball screens. We’ve had some awesome days in practice and today was maybe a little bit higher than usual, but nothing crazy.”

Gonzaga.summary:
From staff reports

The schedule is set for the new-look Pac-12 women’s basketball season.

The Gonzaga and Washington State teams learned the dates of their conference matchups Friday, the Pac-12 announced. The conference is using the same Wednesday/Saturday and Thursday-Sunday schedule as the men’s games, which were announced Wednesday.

There are 16 games for the eight-team conference with each team playing each other home and away.

Gonzaga opens at home against Oregon State on Jan. 6, while Washington State hosts Texas State on Jan. 9. Times and TV information are to be announced.

Conference play concludes on March 6 with Gonzaga hosting WSU at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga holds a 14-7 series lead over WSU and won all four meetings while they played in the West Coast Conference the last two years.

Gonzaga.title: Braden Huff's return and four other things to watch at Gonzaga's Kraziness in the Kennel
Gonzaga.summary:
The exact makeup of Gonzaga’s 2026-27 roster remains unclear one month out from the season opener, but the group of players Mark Few and his staff assembled will take the floor for the first time on Saturday at Kraziness in the Kennel.

The annual preseason showcase, sold out as of Thursday afternoon, will start at 2 p.m. at McCarthey Athletic Center with player introductions followed by hype videos, a 3-point shooting contest, skills contest, intrasquad scrimmage and player/coach speeches. ESPN’s Sean Farnham is emceeing for the third straight year and SWX will carry the live broadcast.

While it’s often difficult to learn much from an abbreviated scrimmage between teammates in the early stages of October, this year’s Kraziness could be more compelling than years past. We break down five of the reasons below.

B-Huff is back

Braden Huff may end up owning a few more Gonzaga scoring and efficiency records by the time his college career ends but he already holds one, posting the top two scoring totals in Kraziness history, with 19 points in 2023 as a true freshman and 17 last season.

Huff’s scoring total won’t necessarily be what fans are focused on when the 6-foot-10 forward takes the floor for the first time since dislocating his kneecap in mid-January, forcing him to miss Gonzaga’s final 17 games in 2025-26.

The real story will be Huff’s strength, mobility and conditioning nine months removed from the injury that prematurely ended his junior season. The crafty forward who led the country in 2-point field goals before his injury has been back on the floor for at least the last two months without any limitations, but the Zags are still slow-playing his return and it’s unclear how many of the 20 minutes he’ll play during Saturday’s scrimmage.

Either way, his return to the floor, and to Gonzaga’s roster, is why many think the Zags will have a chance to play deep into the 2027 NCAA Tournament.

“We’ve been very, very, very conservative with him, especially this summer,” Few told The Spokesman-Review during Naismith Hall of Fame festivities in August. “There’s no need for him to do that. He’s in great shape and looks good.”

Who’s actually available?

This is a question we might be revisiting before both of Gonzaga’s exhibitions, prior to the Nov. 2 opener against Purdue and throughout the early stages of the regular season.

Similar to a handful of schools around the country, Gonzaga continues to wait on eligibility lawsuits and international waiver decisions that will determine whether starters and key rotation players can actually compete this season.

Fifth-year transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida), Javon Bennett (Dayton) and Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State) are currently involved in lawsuits that will determine whether they can suit up, with no real clarity on when verdicts will arrive.

Lee is currently eligible under a temporary restraining order, but still needs a favorable decision from the Superior Court of Santa Clara County on Oct. 20. Bennett and Wiggins earned preliminary injunctions in Ohio and Georgia, but are now ineligible after courts in both states granted an emergency stay motion, revoking the pair’s eligibility until their individual cases are heard.

Spanish forward Izan Almansa is the fourth player in limbo as the Real Madrid product waits on the NCAA to process his international eligibility waiver. Slowly but surely, the sport’s governing body is getting to waivers filed by basketball players and recently approved Gonzaga point guard Nathan De Sousa, a native of France, but Almansa’s wait continues into the first week of October.

All four players are on campus, listed on the web roster Gonzaga published earlier this week and depicted in player posters at the Volkar Center, but Lee, Bennett, Wiggins and Almansa haven’t been formally announced by the school at this point, nor have they been featured in social media photos shared by the basketball program.

Will the quartet of players participate in Kraziness? Outside of Huff’s return, it’s probably the most intriguing storyline leading into this year’s event. For reference, Tyon Grant-Foster obtained a practice waiver that enabled him to take part in Kraziness last year while the NCAA reviewed his eligibility case. When Grant-Foster’s eligibility waiver was denied the following week, his practice waiver became inactive.

Diop’s debut

Between unexpected point guard issues, 5-in-5 court cases and looming uncertainty around international transfers, it’s easy to forget Gonzaga’s offseason started with a bang in the transfer portal.

The Zags won a high-stakes bidding war with Rick Pitino and St. John’s for 7-foot Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop, widely considered to be the top center available during the most recent portal cycle.

Diop is technically listed at 7-1 and 245 pounds on GU’s new roster and Zag fans will have a chance to see the towering sophomore in person for the first time – or at least for the first time since last November, when he had 11 points, four rebounds and two blocks in a 77-65 loss to his new teammates in Tempe, Arizona.

“We haven’t had somebody like him,” Few said. “So big, so athletic, lob-catcher, rim-protector. Maybe (Ronny) Turiaf or somebody would be the closest one we’ve had over the years, I’d have to think about that. Great personality, plays with joy but also kind of work in progress.”

The Zags are hopeful Diop can impact the game on both ends of the floor, but defensive rim protection could be his most valuable asset to this team, considering the offensive firepower they’ll have elsewhere, particularly with Huff and sophomore wing Davis Fogle.

First day of school (and Kraziness)

The impact of Gonzaga’s freshman class could largely hinge on the eligibility of the four players we mentioned earlier, but all three of Luca Foster, Sam Funches and Juwan Ekanga should get significant run Saturday afternoon in a scrimmage setting.

While this may not be considered one of Gonzaga’s best freshman classes, it definitely is not among the worst either. Foster, Funches and Ekanga make up a well-rounded group consisting of two top-50 high school prospects that selected Few’s program over a handful of power conference suitors and an intriguing international prospect who’s already played games in France’s top professional league.

It’s also a good time to remind fans Fogle wasn’t projected to play a high-usage role for the Zags in the lead-up to Kraziness last year, let alone crack the team’s rotation at any point. Injuries and inconsistent play from others at his position eventually made Fogle the team’s sixth man and the freshman wing went on to average double figures the final two months of the season.

If all three 5-in-5 transfers and Almansa are eligible to compete this year, it’s unlikely Gonzaga would have to lean heavily on its freshman class, but last season reaffirmed how quickly things can change.

In any event, Saturday’s scrimmage gives Foster, Funches and Ekanga the chance to show how they’ve developed since arriving on campus and perhaps which of the three would be best-equipped to step into Gonzaga’s rotation if the situation calls for it.

Roebuck returns

The Zags have a solid hit rate when it comes to signing recruits who visit campus during Kraziness weekend.

They picked up a commitment from Funches within a week of last year’s event, signed four-star guard Dusty Stromer months after his visit in 2022 and, most notably, went 4-for-4 with Jalen Suggs, Chet Holmgren, Julian Strawther and Dominick Harris after the group of four- and five-star prospects traveled to Spokane in 2019.

Another important recruiting weekend is in store for the Zags, with four-star guard Gene Roebuck returning to the Kennel for his official visit. Roebuck traveled from La Mirada, California, last year for an unofficial visit that coincided with GU’s opener, but the 45th-ranked player in the class of 2027 is returning to Spokane after taking official visits to California and Washington earlier this fall.

A 6-foot-4, 180-pound combo guard, Roebuck is a consensus four-star prospect according to major recruiting services, the No. 9-ranked guard in the class and No. 4-ranked player in California.

The Zags currently have one player, five-star guard Dooney Johnson, committed in the 2027 class. Five-star guard Jalen Davis, a Bremerton High School standout, is also scheduled to take an official visit to the Kennel on Nov. 7 for GU’s nonconference game against New Mexico State.

Gonzaga.title: Denver Nuggets sign former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard to two-way contract
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard is on the move for the third time this offseason.

Nembhard, who was traded from the Dallas Mavericks to the Atlanta Hawks on July 19 before being shipped to the Charlotte Hornets last week, has seemingly found a permanent landing spot for the 2026-27 season after signing a two-way contract with the Denver Nuggets.

The second-year pro will team up with former Gonzaga wing Julian Strawther in Denver and split time between the NBA’s Nuggets and G League Grand Rapids Gold in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Denver waived guard KJ Simpson to open up a two-way spot for Nembhard.

It becomes the fourth team for Nembhard since a two-game stint with the Mavericks this July at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas. Days after his second Summer League game, Nembhard was involved in a three-team trade that sent the former Zag to Atlanta in exchange for Zaccharie Risacher. The Hawks also acquired Oklahoma City guard Lu Dort as part of the deal.

Nembhard’s time with Atlanta lasted just two months before the Hawks traded the point guard, Buddy Hield and cash considerations to Charlotte for forward Dorian Finney-Smith. Within days of that move, reports indicated that Charlotte intended to waive Nembhard before training camp, making him an unrestricted free agent.

The Mavericks signed Nembhard to an undrafted two-way deal last summer and leaned on the point guard throughout the regular season. Nembhard’s two-way contract was converted to a standard deal late in the season and the rookie made 60 appearances for Dallas, including 27 starts.

Nembhard, who broke Gonzaga’s single-season assists record in each of his two seasons with the program, averaged 6.6 points, 5.3 assists and 2.2 rebounds for the Mavericks while shooting 41.5% from the field, 35.6% from the 3-point line and 80.6% from the free throw line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga unveils full 2026-27 schedule, will open Pac-12 season with rivalry matchup at WSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s inaugural Pac-12 season is right around the corner and might feel even closer now that the Bulldogs have a full regular-season schedule to parse through.

The Pac-12 Conference revealed its men’s basketball schedule on Wednesday, allowing Gonzaga to formally announce its complete 31-game regular-season slate featuring at least 15 nonconference games and 16 more as part of the Pac-12’s double round-robin format.

There weren’t any new developments with Gonzaga’s nonleague slate, which has been pieced together over the last handful of months and includes at least 10 games against high-major opponents. The Zags could potentially play an 11th power-conference foe, and 16th nonconference game, if they qualify for the championship game at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

Gonzaga will have to get through a new batch of opponents to win its first Pac-12 championship, but Mark Few’s team will open conference play against a familiar foe when it travels to Pullman on Jan. 6 for the 155th all-time meeting with Washington State.

The conference home opener is scheduled for Jan. 9 against Colorado State, followed by a Jan. 13 road test at Fresno State.

Gonzaga returns home on Jan. 16 for one of its most-anticipated matchups in the new Pac-12, pitting Few against Boise State and longtime Zags assistant Leon Rice. The game also doubles as a reunion for the Few family with AJ Few, the oldest son of Gonzaga’s Hall of Fame coach, entering his second season on Boise State’s staff as a director of player personnel.

After the Boise State matchup, Gonzaga will be back on the road for a two-game swing against Utah State (Jan. 21) and Oregon State (Jan. 24). The Aggies are targeting a fifth straight NCAA Tournament appearance under their fourth different coach and announced a sellout for the Gonzaga game two weeks before the schedule was released.

Three days later, the Zags will face another first-year coach, Oregon State’s Justin Joyner, in Corvallis, Oregon. Joyner was an assistant coach for Michigan’s national title-winning team last season and had the scouting report when the Wolverines thumped Gonzaga 101-61 in the Players Era championship.

Gonzaga won’t leave the state of Washington for its next three games, hosting Fresno State on Jan. 27 before traveling to Seattle on Jan. 30 for a nonleague matchup with Oregon at Climate Pledge Arena. The Zags return home on Feb. 4 for their first-ever meeting with Texas State, which left the Sun Belt Conference to join the revamped Pac-12.

Two more intriguing road games follow for Gonzaga, which travels to play San Diego State at Viejas Arena before a return game with Boise State on Feb. 10 at ExtraMile Arena.

The Zags travel back to Spokane for a single game against Washington State on Feb. 17 before leaving for another nonconference game on Feb. 20 against Duke at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

Gonzaga will stay on the road to play Texas State in San Marcos on Feb. 25 before returning to the Inland Northwest for a two-game home swing against San Diego State (Feb. 27) and Oregon State (March 3). The team’s Pac-12 regular-season finale will take place on March 6 at Colorado State.

The Pac-12 Tournament opens just three days later at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, but Gonzaga could avoid playing on March 9, 10 or 11 if the Zags are able to secure a No. 1 or 2 seed and earn a bye to the Pac-12 semifinals on March 12. The conference championship game will take place on March 13 and air on CBS/Paramount+.

Tipoff times and television broadcast details for the majority of Gonzaga’s nonconference games, and all 16 conference games, will be announced in the coming weeks.

Under the new Pac-12 schedule, all nine teams are playing 16 games, with home and road matchups against each of the other eight schools. No team is playing three consecutive road games or four of five games on the road and every team is opening and closing its conference schedule with one home and road game across its first and final two contests.

Zags add exhibition

Gonzaga’s preseason exhibition schedule will start on Oct. 24 against Arkansas and resume four days later with a home matchup against NAIA opponent Lewis-Clark State.

A tipoff time and television details for the Oct. 28 exhibition have yet to be announced.

The Lewiston-based school has been a common exhibition opponent for Gonzaga, with the Zags and Warriors meeting as recently as 2023-24, when Graham Ike scored 24 points and Braden Huff added 21 to help Few’s team pull away for a 96-58 win.

Ferris High School product Dylan Skaife returns to LCSC’s roster after starting in all 32 games for the Warriors as a sophomore.
