Washington State.title: What role has WSU's offensive line played in the Cougars' struggling offense?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Ashton Tripp is a man of few words, a giant Washington State offensive lineman whose height belies his desire to chat. He’s been around the Cougars’ program for more than three years now, and in his second year starting at left tackle, he’s never been long on words.

So it follows that Tripp, a 6-foot-7 product of Kennewick, has been succinct in summarizing his WSU offense’s struggles so far.

“After watching the tape, I mean, it’s disappointing for sure,” Tripp said on Monday. “We gotta play 11 as one. I know it’s cliche, but that’s just how it’s gotta be. Here and there, it’s always one guy off, so we just gotta click.”

Much has been made of WSU’s offensive woes, the struggles from quarterback Caden Pinnick that have played an outsize role in his team’s 1-4 start to the season, especially his offense’s output of 11.8 points per game – No. 130 nationally. Headed into a Friday night matchup with Utah State, an evening kickoff in Logan, coach Kirby Moore is taking over playcalling duties to try and revive a moribund outfit.

Pinnick has shouldered much of the blame, and plenty has been deserved. He’s thrown an interception in all five games, and he’s lost six total turnovers, accounting for the majority of the Cougs’ nine total turnovers. On Monday, Moore seemed to indicate that he is open to making a change at that position, perhaps moving toward redshirt sophomore Julian Dugger or redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman.

“Everyone’s gonna get reps,” Moore said. “I think that’s the most important thing. Everyone’s gotta make the reps count. We’ll see where it’s at on Friday, and we’ll play ball.”

On the topic of WSU’s scuffling offense, here is a subplot that has gone a little understated: How has the Cougars’ offensive line played? Tripp has acquitted himself well, but things haven’t gone as smoothly on other parts of their front five, leading coaches to make a few personnel changes after WSU’s road loss to Kansas State last month.

In the three games since, coaches have rolled with this group: Tripp at left tackle, Jonny Lester at left guard, Noah Dunham at center, Nick Bakken at right guard and Jaylin Caldwell at right tackle. At the beginning of the season, Lester was playing right tackle, but after the K-State game, left guard Kyle Martin was benched, prompting Lester to move to left guard – where he started last season – and pulling Caldwell off the bench to play right tackle.

Could WSU make changes to that group? Moore has said that everything with the Cougars’ offense is up for reevaluation, which could open up the door for veteran tackle Maximus McCree, whose transfer was hailed as a key acquisition for WSU back in January. A former starter at Washington, he has yet to play a snap at WSU.

As currently constructed, how has WSU’s offensive line fared? In WSU’s 26-6 loss to Fresno State last weekend, Pinnick took five sacks, giving him 18 on the season, which ranks No. 129 of 138 FBS teams nationally. But interestingly, Pro Football Focus only dinged the Cougars’ offensive line for three of those, indicating that Pinnick was responsible for the other two. That would add up to the eye test, which has affirmed that Pinnick’s pocket presence ranks highly on his list of problems.

In fact, here’s a key trend to consider: PFF has a stat called QB-fault pressures, which are basically what they sound like. In simplest terms, these are sacks that PFF determines were the QB’s fault rather than the offensive line’s – he ran himself into pressure, held onto the ball too long, something of that sort.

Pinnick ranks first nationally with 10 QB-fault sacks.

That goes a long way in explaining some patterns, like his inability to make timely decisions and find the right balance of staying in the pocket too long and bailing too quickly. But to a certain degree, it absolves the Cougars’ offensive line of blame, revealing Pinnick to be more of a culprit for his own sacks than the men charged with protecting him.

But the Cougars’ front five haven’t been perfect, either. Dunham has been the least responsible for QB pressures, according to PFF, only 9% of the pressures Pinnick has faced coming from his assignments. That lines up with his season as a whole, earning the offensive line’s top pass-blocking grade (65.9) and only six pressures total.

Most of the pressure Pinnick has faced has come from the right side, with Bakken and Caldwell sharing about 22% each of pressures. Lester has the same rate, while the lowest belongs to Tripp, at just 17%.

What about run-blocking? Another reason the Cougars are struggling on offense is their lack of a credible running game. In the second half against Fresno State, tailbacks Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi combined for just five carries. This week, Moore emphasized the need to incorporate them more into the Cougs’ offense.

The highest-graded run-blocker on the WSU offensive line is Lester, who has earned a grade of 74.6, well above average. Next is Caldwell at 61.1, while Bakken is at 60.1, Dunham is at 55.3 and Tripp checks in at the lowest grade with 51.6. It’s important to note that Lester, Dunham and Tripp were all recruited to play in a much different offense, much closer to the Air Raid of old than the approach these current Cougs are taking.

“It’s just all about us. I just keep coming back to it,” Tripp said. “We gotta just keep doing more. We gotta keep working, keep doing extra stuff, get the guys together, and we gotta start clicking.”

Washington State.title: Sizzling Oregon State, struggling WSU and eligibility complications | Pac-12 bowl projections
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 bowl selection process in 2026 treats the former conference as if it never imploded, grouping the 12 legacy schools together just as it did the previous two years. Meanwhile, the new Pac-12 teams have separate postseason arrangements. To simplify the situation, we have split the 18 teams into two groups: Pac-12 legacy bowls and Pac-12 new bowls. Washington State and Oregon State are part of the legacy bowl process with the exception of the Poinsettia Bowl. 

So low was the bar for Oregon State this fall that its 3-2 record constitutes an upside surprise of the highest order.

Whether it’s the closer-than-expected losses or the resounding wins, the dazzling aerial game or coach JaMarcus Shephard’s unstoppable enthusiasm, the Beavers have produced a riveting narrative entering the midway point of the season.

They have also turned trigonometry into basic multiplication.

Oregon State’s bowl math is easy enough to compute: If they win three of the seven remaining games, the Beavers will participate in the postseason for the first time since 2023 and the fourth time in the past decade.

But which bowl?

That’s where the situation turns complicated because the Beavers, like fellow Pac-12 holdover Washington State, are eligible for two sets of games: The legacy Pac-12 bowls and the new Pac-12 bowls.

And for the College Football Playoff, of course.

That sentence might have read like fantasy in August but is worth brief mention here. If the Beavers somehow run the table, win the Pac-12 and finish 11-2, with competitive losses to Texas Tech and Houston and at least one victory over Boise State, they would receive consideration for the Group of Six berth in the CFP.

That scenario has a non-zero chance of materializing, but not by much.

According to projections on teamrankings.com, the wagering and analytics website, the likelihood of Oregon State winning out is about 2 percent.

But what if the Beavers finish 7-5 or 8-4? Where might they land? More significantly, would they be placed in the pool of legacy Pac-12 games or new Pac-12 games?

The key elements to the process are as follows:

• The legacy Pac-12 teams are eligible for (in order) the Alamo, Las Vegas, Holiday, Sun, Poinsettia and Independence Bowls.

• The six new Pac-12 teams are eligible for the Poinsettia and Hawaii Bowls, plus a pool of ESPN games.

• Oregon State and Washington State will participate on the legacy Pac-12 side of all games except the Poinsettia pairing, where they are considered new Pac-12 teams.

• The Pac-12 legacy bowls select first, meaning the Beavers likely would land in a legacy game if they are 8-4 or 9-3. If they only win six or seven games, there’s a chance they would not be picked for the legacy games and move over to the Poinsettia or Hawaii Bowls.

• Don’t forget about the one-win-down rule, which allows any of the legacy bowls to pass one team in favor of another as long as there is no more than a one-game difference in record. The Holiday Bowl, for example, could pass on the Beavers at 8-4 in favor of Washington at 7-5 but not if the Huskies are 6-6.

That policy could work against the Beavers because of their small media market and low national profile.

It could work in favor of the Beavers if bowl executives prioritize ticket sales and Oregon State fans are considered likely to attend the game en masse.

Even if we knew Oregon State’s final record, projecting a landing spot would be exceedingly difficult because of the myriad factors involved.

Also, we don’t know how many, if any, legacy Pac-12 teams will jump into the CFP, thereby opening spots in the non-playoff games. If Utah and/or Oregon qualify, everyone below them in the pecking order moves up.

However, it’s reasonable to assume only a handful of legacy Pac-12 teams will finish with eight or more wins based on current records and upcoming schedules.

If the Beavers are 9-3 or 8-4, they would be well positioned for the Holiday or Sun Bowls.

Why not the Alamo or Las Vegas? Both could be options, but the one-win-down rule might prompt the bowls to select one of the Los Angeles schools.

If the Beavers are 7-5, the Sun or Independence Bowls would come into play.

Only at 6-6 would a berth in Poinsettia, as a new Pac-12 team, become the most realistic option.

In some ways, that might be the most interesting matchup. We would love to see Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree face Washington or Arizona.

To the bowl projections …

Pac-12 legacy bowls

College Football Playoff: Utah (Big 12 champion)

Comment: The Utes (4-0) could qualify for the CFP through the at-large pool if they finish with one loss. (It’s tough to envision a two-loss Big 12 team getting the requisite respect from the selection committee.) For the moment, we view Utah as the team to beat in the conference, particularly with Texas Tech looking vulnerable on a weekly basis.

College Football Playoff: Oregon (Big Ten at-large)

Comment: The Ducks (3-1) have eight games remaining, one loss in their pocket and a date in Columbus looming. At 10-2, an at-large bid should be forthcoming, although they might not be seeded high enough to host an opening-round game.

Alamo Bowl: UCLA

Comment: There is a good chance the UCLA-USC duel at the end of the season determines bowl destinations for both teams, with the winner receiving the more prestigious assignment. Given the upcoming schedules, the Bruins (4-0) have a better chance to sneak into the CFP, but the best non-playoff bowl is the most likely option at this point.

Las Vegas Bowl: USC

Comment: The schedule includes Wisconsin, Indiana and UCLA on the road and Ohio State at home. Those teams are a combined 17-2. Even if the Trojans (5-1) split that brutal quartet, they would finish with three losses. And the committee has never invited a 9-3 team to the playoff party.

Holiday Bowl: Oregon State

Comment: The Beavers (3-2) would celebrate a bowl bid anywhere. Yuma, Elko, Yakima – sign them up! But San Diego against an ACC opponent? Corvallis would become a ghost town the last week of December.

Sun Bowl: Arizona

Comment: Don’t dismiss the Wildcats (4-1) as a title contender in the Big 12 race, particularly after they whacked Cincinnati. But if they don’t reach Arlington, options could be limited: The L.A. schools might have priority for the Alamo and Las Vegas Bowls (TV markets), and Arizona was in the Holiday last year.

Poinsettia Bowl: Washington

Comment: A victory over Iowa on Friday night is important but not critical for the bowl math given the spate of winnable games remaining. But the reeling Huskies (3-2) won’t be a popular pick on the bowl circuit. Executives always favor teams with energized, not depressed, fans.

Independence Bowl: Arizona State

Comment: The Hotline supercomputer ran 10,000 simulations and spit out a 6-6 record for the Sun Devils 5,001 times. Just kidding. We don’t have a supercomputer. But we do have eyes. And from what we saw of Arizona State (2-2) over the weekend, six wins looks right.

Non-qualifier: Cal

Comment: Had you mapped the worst possible scenario for a new coach in Berkeley, it would effectively match Tosh Lupoi’s opening month. The Bears (2-3) will be lucky to win five games, much less six or seven.

Non-qualifier: Colorado

Comment: The Buffaloes (2-3) are averaging 10.3 points per game against FBS opponents. Barring a court order that gives Shedeur Sanders additional eligibility, the trajectory won’t change enough for CU to win four of the remaining seven.

Non-qualifier: Stanford

Comment: We aren’t aware of an NCAA policy banning any team that loses to Wake Forest by 54 points from participating in the postseason. But it would make more sense than most of the organization’s rules. In our view , Stanford (2-3) is essentially playing for 2028.

Non-qualifier: Washington State

Comment: First-year coach Kirby Moore is taking over play-calling duties for the struggling Cougars (1-4), which essentially means he picked the wrong offensive coordinator and the wrong quarterback. At least Moore got the defense right with coordinator Trent Bray.

Pac-12 new bowls

College Football Playoff: Boise State

Comment: At this point, the Broncos (4-1) hold the pole position in the race for the Group of Six spot in the playoff, with New Mexico, James Madison and Toledo as the top competition. Yes, North Dakota State is undefeated, but we aren’t convinced the Bison warrant that level of respect. Their schedule has been pillowy soft.

Poinsettia Bowl: Fresno State

Comment: A morsel of clarity will come to the Pac-12 race Saturday night when the Bulldogs (4-1) host Boise State in the first of three games matching the presumptive title contenders. And for what it’s worth, Fresno State also gets Oregon State at home.

Hawaii Bowl: San Diego State

Comment: The Aztecs (2-3) showed enough grit to beat Texas State, despite a roster torched by injury and illness (i.e., the mumps outbreak), that we have upgraded their forecast. But to make the bowl math work, they might need help from the conference’s Flex schedule. Five wins entering the final weekend is a distinct possibility.

Non-qualifier: Colorado State

Comment: If Jim Mora had changed defensive playcallers prior to the UTSA game, the Rams (2-3) might be on the high side of .500 right now and in prime position for a bowl berth. They have more than enough offense to secure six wins.

Non-qualifier: Texas State

Comment: The loss in San Diego, to a depleted opponent, could cost the Bobcats (2-3) a bowl bid. Of course, we could say the same about their come-from-ahead defeat to UTSA, as well.

Non-qualifier: Utah State

Comment: The Hotline saw a comment from Nevada coach Jeff Choate about the Mountain West being superior to the Pac-12. At the top, New Mexico could very well be a match for Boise State. But the middle and bottom tiers of the Pac-12, including Utah State (1-4), are far superior. Just check the scoreboard.

Washington State.title: Gap between WSU, conference leaders looks massive | Pac-12 power rankings Week 6
Washington State.summary:
Editor’s note: The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday and consider both the latest results and seasonlong performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

One week into round-robin play, it’s abundantly clear: The Pac-12 is a three-team race.

Boise State, Oregon State and Fresno State are the class of the conference, and it doesn’t appear to be particularly close. The gap between the top three and bottom five feels like a chasm.

Washington State doesn’t have enough offense to secure a bowl berth, much less contend for a spot in the Pac-12 championship game.

Colorado State doesn’t have enough defense. (Nor do the Rams have a defensive coordinator at the moment).

San Diego State? The Aztecs are lacking the most essential ingredient: healthy bodies.

Texas State doesn’t do anything well enough, which is doubly true when it comes to holding second-half leads.

Utah State does everything poorly.

That’s it. Remove those five flawed teams, and you have three remaining.

They aren’t created equal, not by any stretch: The Beavers lead with their offense, the Bulldogs with their defense and the Broncos with both, which explains their status as the frontrunner for both the Pac-12 title and a berth in the College Football Playoff.

But the beauty of the rebuilt Pac-12’s small size is the pure round-robin schedule. We don’t have to imagine how one contender would fare against another or delay judgment until the conference championship game.

In the Big 12, Utah and BYU don’t play Texas Tech.

In the SEC, Alabama and Georgia don’t play Texas.

In the Big Ten, Oregon doesn’t play Indiana.

But the Pac-12 doesn’t have that problem with eight teams and seven league games.

Everyone plays everyone, allowing us to identify the defining dates:

Oct. 10: Boise State at Fresno State

Oct. 31: Oregon State at Fresno State

Nov. 14: Oregon State at Boise State

Advantage to the Bulldogs, right? They host the other two while Oregon State is on the road for both.

Not necessarily.

Oregon State has played well away from home, with blowout victories at UTEP and Colorado State and a competitive loss at Houston.

Boise State can win anywhere.

Here are the victory projections for each team against the other two, according to the gambling and analytics website TeamRankings.com:

• Boise State: 66.3% at Fresno State and 77.4% against Oregon State

• Fresno State: 36.7% against Boise State and 59% against Oregon State

• Oregon State: 22.6% at Boise State and 41% at Fresno State

Our hunch: The Broncos win both, the Beavers split and the Bulldogs get swept.

As the late, great philosopher Bill Walton said often, “Offense wins championships.”

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (4-1/1-0)

Result: beat Utah State 37-18

Next up: at Fresno State (7:30 p.m. on the CW)

Comment: No team in the conference has better balance than the Broncos – not only offense-defense balance but also run-pass balance: They are averaging 227 rushing yards and 212 passing yards per game and likely will need every bit of both Saturday night against the Bulldogs, who allow just 16 points per game. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (3-2/1-0)

Result: won at Colorado State 56-26

Next up: vs. San Diego State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Receiver Jesse Legree falls into the same where-did-they-find-that-guy category as former Oregon State stars like Brandin Cooks and Jacquizz Rodgers. (The answer is Baltimore). But as the heart of conference play ramps up and opponents develop a better sense for OSU’s scheme and formations, we wonder: How will the Beavers adjust to the adjustments? (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (4-1/1-0)

Result: won at Washington State 26-6

Next up: vs. Boise State (7:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The Bulldogs were set up to fail in the season opener at USC, which had already played (San Jose State) and was far sharper. Since that 39-0 loss, Fresno State is allowing 10.8 points per game. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (2-3/0-1)

Result: lost to Oregon State 56-26

Next up: idle

Comment: It’s not often that a coordinator is stripped of his playcalling duties during a game. But if you had asked us to name the three Pac-12 head coaches most likely to make that type of in-game decision, Jim Mora Jr. would have been among our group. (Granted, relieving Tyson Summers of his responsibilities was a competitive imperative). (Last week: 4)

5. San Diego State (2-3/1-0)

Result: beat Texas State 31-29

Next up: at Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: An indisputably impressive victory for the Aztecs considering their two tailbacks were injured, more than a dozen players were unavailable due to the mumps outbreak and quarterback Jayden Denegal has struggled under any and every condition this season. And yet, the Aztecs rallied from a 14-point deficit thanks to their defense and special teams. (Last week: 7)

6. Texas State (2-3/0-1)

Result: lost at San Diego State 31-29

Next up: idle

Comment: The Bobcats were outscored 52-21 after halftime in losses to UTSA and San Diego State, dropping the former by five points and the latter by two. Had they held on, the season would have an entirely different look and feel. But one of the defining features of mediocre teams is the inability to close out games. (Last week: 5)

7. Washington State (1-4/0-1)

Result: lost to Fresno State 26-6

Next up: at Utah State (Friday at 6 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: From here, it’s clear that first-year coach Kirby Moore, a former receiver and offensive coordinator, has no answers. He announced Monday that he will take over the offensive playcalling duties. It’s clear that if Moore doesn’t fix the offensive offense in the next 19 games, Washington State will be in the market for a new coach. Time is short when attempting to prove you belong in the Power Four. (Last week: 6)

8. Utah State (1-4/0-1)

Result: lost at Boise State 37-18

Next up: vs. Washington State (Friday at 6 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: One team will collect its second victory of the season Friday night in Logan, but the process could be tough on the eyes and set the sport back years. First team to 11 wins. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: 5 lingering thoughts from WSU's loss to Fresno State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – At some point in the Gesa Field locker room, not long after his Washington State team managed just six points in an anemic loss to Fresno State on Saturday evening, Kirby Moore got his players together and left them with a message.

“We talked about, naturally, there’s gonna be noise, and rightfully so,” Moore said. “We gotta have a better product on the field. We all agree that we’re a better football team than that. The leadership group’s gotta step up, and the only way I know how to improve is to go back to work.”

Plenty of that will be in order for the Cougars, who are now 1-4 overall and 0-1 in Pac-12 play to begin Moore’s tenure. With this 26-6 setback, WSU’s offense now ranks near the bottom in the country in several key departments. With this sampling, keep in mind that there are 138 FBS teams this season.

• 11.8 points per game, No. 130

• 27% on third down, No. 133

• 287 yards per game, No. 133

• 18 sacks allowed, No. 129

• 11 red zone attempts, No. 125

Here are two more statistics that might best capture the Cougars’ struggles on offense. They’re averaging 2.8 yards per rush, which is No. 128 nationally. They’re also averaging 5.6 yards per pass attempt, which is two spots up from dead last in the country.

The eye-test backs up those trends. Quarterback Caden Pinnick, who threw an interception to bring him to six total turnovers on the season, hasn’t shown much acumen with the deep ball. Credit WSU coaches for game-planning around that, but they also aren’t getting much out of their running game, which could play a key role in opening up the field for their quarterback.

In short, that’s how you end up with this WSU offense, which has now gone without an offensive touchdown twice in one season. For the Cougars, that’s the first time that has happened since 2008, the first season of former coach Paul Wulff’s tenure. Wulff actually did visit Moore and coaches back in August, but in terms of on-field results, that’s not company anyone with WSU’s program wants to keep.

Here are five lingering thoughts from WSU’s loss to Fresno State.

1. Caden Pinnick’s pocket presence leaves a lot to be desired: Pinnick’s list of issues is quite lengthy, but this problem ranks somewhere near the top: He doesn’t look entirely comfortable in the pocket, whether or not he’s seeing pressure. He may have taken five sacks, but Pro Football Focus only dinged the Cougars’ offensive line for one, which does a great job of crystallizing the issue.

On one play late in the first quarter, Fresno State brought a blitzer up to the line of scrimmage a few seconds before the snap, and Pinnick seemed to be aware of that. The WSU player he was lined up against, tight end Jack Pedersen, even pointed to him. But defensive back Loyall Mouzon came unblocked just the same, and even with a second to get the ball out to running back Maxwell Woods in the flat, Pinnick elected to hold on to the ball and take the sack.

At the beginning of the third quarter, Pinnick also put on display what is becoming a bigger and bigger issue: He won’t throw the ball away. On this play, he does well to fake a handoff and make one defender miss, but he’s out of the pocket so he has a chance to throw it away and avoid a loss. Instead, he takes a sack for a loss of 10 yards. The Cougars punted three plays later.

Let’s fast forward to the end of the third quarter, when WSU was facing a 13-6 deficit. Backed up deep in their own territory, the Cougars go with a shotgun dropback for Pinnick, who gets great protection from his O-line. He chose to scramble from the pocket, which looked unnecessary, and checked it down for a short gain.

On that play, it wasn’t just Pinnick’s decision to bail from a clean pocket that presented a problem. That choice spawned another: Pedersen was called for holding. That’s the kind of penalty that quarterbacks put their blockers at risk of when they scramble from the pocket, causing blockers to become more visible to officials.

2. Matyus McLain turned in his best game yet: In his fifth game at the FBS level, the defensive end McLain looked like the best version of himself. For the game, he totaled four tackles, including a half-sack and two tackles for loss, playing a key role in the Cougar defense keeping the team in the game.

Late in the first quarter, McLain shot through the line of scrimmage and dragged down running back Rayshon Luke for a loss of four. Then, late in the third frame, he made back-to-back huge plays: He brought down Fresno State QB Jayden Mandal for his half-sack, sharing it with defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele.

Only moments later, he dropped back in coverage and made a key third-down tackle in space, highlighting the athleticism that makes him so dangerous in the pass-rush department.

3. Jack Stevens is back in business: It wasn’t long ago when WSU kicker Jack Stevens was mired in a long streak of misses, entering last week’s game against Arizona 1-for-5 on field goals. There was a lot wrong with the Cougars’ entire field goal operation, which caused one last week to get blocked, and a lot has changed since.

The most important centers on Stevens, who connected on two field goals in Saturday’s game, including a careerlong 50-yarder to tie the game right before halftime. He looked psyched afterwards. You can tell his confidence is returning, which could aid a struggling WSU offense.

Credit WSU coaches for making changes up front. They removed usual right tackle Jaylin Caldwell, whose failure to block anyone last week resulted in a blocked field goal, as well as offensive lineman Arion Williams, who were a part of that blocked field goal. They subbed in linemen Kyle Martin and Nick Bakken, which helped facilitate a cleaner operation.

4. Why did WSU almost completely abandon the running game in the second half? For the game, Cougar running backs Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for 45 yards on 12 carries. In the second half, those numbers dropped significantly: Those three combined for just 13 yards on five carries. As a team, the Cougars posted negative-4 rushing yards in the second half.

You read that right: In the second half of Saturday’s game, WSU’s stable of running backs – whose retention was hailed as one of Moore’s top offseason accomplishments – got only five tries to run the ball. The Cougars almost entirely shelved the running game, resulting in 18 passes for 70 total yards.

What’s even weirder is that Woods, who turned in a 7-yard carry early in the game, played only 12 snaps. In the second quarter, he ran backwards to look for more space, which became a 4-yard loss. Maybe that explains his low snap count, but considering his shiftiness and speed, there has to be a bigger role in the Cougs’ offense for Woods – and Vorhees and Pulalasi.

5. Did Julian Dugger or Owen Eshelman deserve a few garbage-time snaps? Pinnick never came out of Saturday’s game, not even in the final three minutes, when the game was out of reach. He had thrown an interception on the previous series, and with only minutes left in a blowout, it seemed possible for WSU coaches to give snaps to one of their other quarterbacks, Dugger or Eshelman.

Instead, Moore rolled with Pinnick, explaining that decision this way: “With where we were at, just the rhythm. Wanted to keep him going with the first group from an offensive line standpoint. But I think everything on offense, we gotta reevaluate.”

It’s clear that Moore wants to stick with his guy, wants to ensure that Pinnick feels like QB1. But Pinnick could still have been QB1 even if coaches gave the game’s final snaps to another quarterback, if only to demonstrate to fans that, yes, they are interested in trying new things.

As WSU prepares for its next game, a road test at Utah State on Friday, it’ll be fascinating to see how Moore talks about the way he’s handling Pinnick and the team’s QB situation.

Washington State.title: Washington State's offense shut down in loss to Fresno State | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — The boo birds rained down on Gesa Field like volcanic ash on scorched terrain, directed at all the men responsible for Washington State’s latest anemic showing, from the head coach to the quarterback to the offensive coordinator to the running backs who couldn’t free themselves, no matter which angle they tried, left or right or forwards or backwards.

Early on in WSU’s second straight loss, a 26-6 home setback to Fresno State to open competition in the rebuilt Pac-12, frustration was already beginning to set in. Quarterback Caden Pinnick was missing throws. Receivers were running routes short of first-down markers. They couldn’t handle a shotgun snap and lost a fumble.

So WSU coach Kirby Moore heard about it from the crowd at Gesa Field, where the Cougars generated 182 yards of total offense in this loss, losing two turnover and going 3-for-14 on third down. WSU slogged through six three-and-outs, too. In their fourth loss of the season, the Cougars showed almost no ability to move the ball, turning in one of the most ghastly offensive showings in program history.

With this performance, WSU now has three offensive touchdowns in four games against FBS competition.

For the game, Pinnick completed 21 of 34 passes for 152 yards and an interception, his worst showing of the season, but the Cougars’ lack of execution also lost them this game. Pinnick, who was sacked seen times, couldn’t throw the ball away when opportunities surfaced. On one third-down pass late in the game, he threw behind tight end Jack Pedersen. On one earlier in the game, Pinnick threw short of wideout Branden Ganashamoorthy.

Above all, it amounted to the kind of listless offensive showing that rarely shows up at Washington State, which is known for fun offenses: The Air Raid, the run-and-shoot, quarterbacks throwing for 500 yards a game, running backs breaking into the open field. Here on Saturday night, WSU tailbacks Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for 45 total rushing yards.

It was also the second time this season WSU has failed to score an offensive touchdown. Before the first time this season, which came in the Cougars’ road loss to Kansas State, the last time that happened to this program was in 2010. Back then, WSU’s coach was Paul Wulff.

The Cougars did produce two scoring drives in this game, both of which resulted in field goals from kicker Jack Stevens, who is beginning to turn things around after a sluggish start to the season. In the second quarter, he hit two field goals, the first a 32-yarder to tie the game at 3-all and the second a 50-yarder — the longest of his career — to tie the game at 6-all right before halftime.

Thanks to WSU’s defense, that was enough to keep the Cougars within one and two scores the entire game. The Cougars were beaten by a handful of Bulldog trick plays — quarterback Jayden Mandal, who connected on 23 of 32 passes for 248 yards, hit a flea-flicker — but they acquitted themselves well otherwise. The Cougs recovered a fumble, and their special-teams unit blocked a field goal, the second time they’ve done that this season.

But the story here on Saturday night was WSU’s offense, which turned in one of the worst outings the program has ever seen. Even in the Cougars’ most forgettable showings in recent memory — a 10-7 loss to Stanford in 2023, a 15-14 loss to Wyoming in 2024, 59-10 loss to North Texas in 2025 — they scored offensive touchdowns. They showed an ability to move the ball. They showed some level of energy, albeit low and listless.

WSU showed almost none of that in Saturday’s game, putting Moore and offensive coordinator Matt Miller under a harsh microscope. Will the Cougars consider a change at QB? What changes will they make in response to this blowout?

WSU returns to action next Friday at Utah State, which is the conference’s only winless team. The Cougars could bounce back in that one, but looking at the way Saturday’s game unfolded, not much will inspire confidence.

BOX SCORE

First quarter

7:01 - FSU 3, WSU 0: Manaki Watanabe makes a 27-yard field goal after the Cougars’ defense stiffens near the goal line.

Second quarter

12:34 - FSU 3, WSU 0: Fresno State quarterback Jayden Mandal fumbles on a QB sneak and WSU’s Khamari Terrell recovers.

9:27 - WSU 3, FSU 3: Jack Stevens makes a 32-yard field goal to tie the score.

6:06 - FSU 6, WSU 3: Watanabe connects on a 22-yard field goal.

0:00 - WSU 6, FSU 6: Stevens hits a career-long 50-yard field goal to even the score.

Halftime

Washington State and Fresno State spent the first half trading field goals.

WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick finished the first half with 82 passing yards, 28 of those yards to his leading receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy.

Fresno State QB Jayden Mandal has passed for 112 yards so far.

Third quarter

9:41 - FSU 13, WSU 6: Josiah Freeman scores the game’s first touchdown on a 3-yard rush.

9:37 FSU 13, WSU 6: FSU recovers a Pinnick fumble and starts its drive on the Cougars’ 24.

Pregame

Washington State is ready to turn the page on the nonconference portion of its schedule, which resulted in a record of 1-3, and welcome new Pac-12 Conference rival Fresno State.

The Bulldogs are riding a three-game win streak after a season-opening loss against USC.

To knock off Fresno State and get back on track toward bowl eligibility, the Cougars will need to take care of the ball and keep quarterback Caden Pinnick in rhythm. The ground game will also be important as WSU may be without running back Kirby Vorhees.

Washington State’s defense will also be able to play with more energy if the offense stays consistent.

Kick off is scheduled for 6:30 p.m. and the TV broadcast can be found on USA.

Series history

Washington State holds a 4-2 advantage over Fresno State, winning the last matchup in 2024 on the road 25-17.

Notable stat

Washington State quarterback Caden Pinnick has a deep passing grade of 32.6, according to Pro Football Focus. Pinnick’s grade is four spots up from last among quarterbacks who have tried at least 13 passes of 20-plus yards.

Washington State.title: Washington State's offense has yet to arrive in new era of Pac-12 | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
This absolutely cannot happen. And it’s happening at the worst possible time.

Washington State’s football team is bad right now. Worse, it is boring.

The home crowd – an especially hardy bunch whose members often undertake long journeys just to get to Pullman for the game because they love their Cougs – were loud with their displeasure after the home offense began the game with three feeble drives.

The Cougars have been bad before, but that was the price paid for playing on the sport’s biggest stage, against its best teams. Fans waited out the bad years with the knowledge that when the Cougars were good, winning the Pac-10 in 1997 and 2002, they were among the nation’s best.

This was not part of the deal. The absolute only silver lining in WSU’s forced relegation to mid-major status was that the Cougars would for the first time not have to survive as the smallest fish in a big pond. That their peers would face similar challenges. And that WSU’s superior tradition and experience at the top would set up the Cougars to be one of the lead schools in the rebuilt Pac-12.

That rebuilt Pac-12, a joint salvation project between WSU and Oregon State, formally kicked off for the Cougars on Saturday night. Now the Cougars are 0-1 all-time in a conference they built and look ready to settle into a familiar place in the standings.

How can fans accept this? How long can they continue to care?

The disingenuous, or possibly just naïve counterpoint would be to say that Fresno State might be good! They entered the game with a 3-1 record and, … I’m sorry, I can’t do it. This is not Pat Hill or Jeff Tedford or Kalen DeBoer’s Fresno State. This team came into the game an underdog to a WSU team that’s only offense is a kicker who finally seems to be getting over his yips.

Make no mistake, the conference hierarchy is being established now. WSU’s natural comparison and rival, Oregon State, isn’t dealing with any of this. The Beavers look great! Beyond that, they are rewriting the rules around talent acquisition in this new era.

WSU, which beat OSU 32-8 the last time they played, has no ability to manufacture explosive plays with wide receiver Tony Freeman out for the season.

OSU, on the other hand is headlined by freshman wide receiver Jessee Legree who is tied for the national lead in receiving touchdowns with Ohio State’s Jeremiah Smith, the best college wide receiver since Randy Moss.

Legree has nine receiving touchdowns so far this season, which is three times as many as every WSU player combined.

This kid is obviously an anomaly, but he’s also a reason OSU is likely to finish near the top of the standings this first year in its new conference. His coaches will be able to tell donors and players that this is a program to invest in. Just look! “Come to Corvallis where you’ll play against mighty Boise State for glory and, if you’re good enough, get big money offers from the schools who passed on you out of high school.”

What is WSU supposed to say?

“Come to Pullman. We still don’t win many games, but you’ve got a great shot at playing time! And the fans won’t boo much longer, they’re almost hoarse.”

What is the solution? I don’t know, I don’t get paid as much as the people who are supposed to find the answers to that. Conference rival Colorado State fired its defensive coordinator in the middle of a game on Saturday, and I can’t imagine anything the Rams defense was doing was as embarrassing as those last five minutes of the WSU game.

But what I do feel qualified to say is there is no structural reason for WSU to look this pathetic. This should be getting easier. The Cougars are in a conference again.

After the original Pac-12 disbanded WSU was in the wilderness for two years. Each year the Cougars made a bowl game, one year reaching as high as No. 18 in the College Football Playoff rankings.

They set themselves up well to start this new era in pole position with rivals they chose. If they can’t give fans something to cheer for soon, they will win this new Pac-12 about as often as they won the old one.

Washington State.title: Why Fresno State will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – By now, you have probably read the statistic that might color Washington State’s Pac-12 opener, a home matchup with Fresno State set for Saturday evening.

Fresno State ranks No. 6 nationally with a turnover margin of plus-seven, while WSU ranks No. 119 with a minus-four.

That paints a fairly accurate picture of the struggles of the Cougars’ offense, which has committed seven turnovers on the season, including five from quarterback Caden Pinnick. They’ve had trouble holding onto the ball, which figures to become even harder to do against a defense that has shown to be one of the country’s finest at jarring it loose.

So while WSU will get what figures to be a more even matchup against Fresno State, making a Cougar win possible, Pinnick has shown that the opponent is not what has prompted some of the bad decisions that have led to his turnovers. He’s made regrettable decisions against the likes of Washington and FCS Duquesne, which is why we’re picking the Bulldogs to walk out of Pullman with a win.

In his first four games at the FBS level, Pinnick has shown to be sharp up to 19 yards out, hitting 49 of 69 of passes (71%) at that depth. And not only has he been less effective at distance, hitting on just 2 of 13 passes on throws of 20-plus yards with two interceptions . It’s becoming clear that when he tries to stretch the field, he’s vulnerable to making mistakes.

For WSU, there’s a way to counter that, which is to generate a credible ground attack. The Cougars are more than capable of doing that, but running back Kirby Vorhees is questionable to play due to an upper-body injury, which would remove one of offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s unit’s best weapons.

Final score: Fresno State 24, WSU 20

Washington State.title: WSU's keys to victory against Fresno State | 2-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State vs. Fresno State

Saturday, 6:30 p.m.

Line: WSU favored by 1½

TV: USA Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU QB Caden Pinnick against Fresno State defense: There’s one theme that will likely shape Saturday’s game: Can Pinnick avoid turnovers against Fresno State’s defense? Pinnick has lost five turnovers for the Cougars, who have committed seven total as a team, adding up to a turnover margin of minus-4. That ranks No. 119 nationally. Meanwhile, Fresno State has engineered a turnover margin of plus-7, which is No. 6 in the country.

Pinnick can’t afford any missteps on Saturday. He’s lost many of his turnovers trying to extend plays and stretch the field, which reinforces what is becoming clear: Pinnick is at his best throwing short and intermediate routes, completing 49 of 69 of passes less than 20 yards, which is a sharp 71%. But he’s much less effective at distance, hitting on just 2 of 13 passes with two interceptions on throws of 20-plus yards.

Fresno State cornerback Simeon Harris, who has pocketed three interceptions already, will be lurking. Pinnick might be able to throw in his direction, but he may be wise to avoid deep throws, which is when he’s gone wrong this fall.

How the Cougs win…

WSU can win this game by generating an effective ground game, which might be complicated by the status of running back Kirby Vorhees, who will be a gametime decision as he nurses an upper-body injury. If Vorhees can’t go, the Cougars could give more carries to redshirt sophomore tailback Maxwell Woods, who has had a similarly rough go against FBS competition this fall.

But against Fresno State, whose defense could be a better matchup for WSU’s offense, Woods and the Cougars could get going. That would simplify things for Pinnick and remove some pressure, allowing him to ease his way into the game, instead of pressing. That’s where he’s gotten in some trouble this season.If WSU can establish a credible ground attack early on Saturday, Pinnick won’t feel the need to create plays that aren’t there, which is often how Fresno State’s defense has feasted in a 3-1 start to the season.

How the Bulldogs win…

Fresno State’s clearest path to victory involves preying on WSU’s biggest weakness, which is its turnovers. By giving Pinnick different looks, the Bulldogs might be able to frustrate the quarterback. Last weekend, Arizona sent a myriad of blitzes at WSU and its offensive line, which couldn’t give Pinnick enough time to make good decisions.

Plus, because of the amount of turnovers the Cougs’ offense has committed, their defense has been on the field for several extra drives and heavy snap counts. WSU’s defense has allowed just 4.3 points per game in the first quarter, which ranks No. 57 nationally. That unit has permitted 11.3 points per game in the fourth quarter, which is No. 123 nationally.That paints a picture of the WSU defense, which has tired out as games unfold. To take full advantage, Fresno State’s defense could engineer long drives against the Cougs’ defense, which is mighty talented. But it’s also made up of human beings, who get tired the more they play.

Key stat: 32.6

Pinnick has earned a Pro Football Focus deep passing grade of 32.6, which is four spots up from dead last in the country among QBs who have tried at least 13 passes of 20-plus yards. That indicates a key limitation of WSU’s offense, which is its inability to create explosive plays through the air. If the Cougars can’t generate explosives on the ground, either, their offense could be in for another forgettable one.

Quotable

“I think any receiver would say one is too many,” wide receiver Darrius Clemons said of his reliability, dropping just one ball this season. “When Caden puts the ball in the air, it’s coming my way, my job is to catch it. He expects me to catch it. I think everybody on the team expects you to catch it. When the ball is in your hands or coming your way, the program’s in your hands, essentially.”

Washington State.title: 'It is surreal': WSU's Jirah Leaupepetele set to square off with brother Jonah of Fresno State
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Sometime on Sunday afternoon, Jirah Leaupepetele pulled out his phone and dialed his brother Jonah. In another week, sometimes the brothers would just be chatting. Or they’d be talking trash to each other, a theme as they grew up together, especially as Jirah has flourished on Washington State’s defensive line and Jonah has landed on Fresno State’s offensive line.

This week, though, Jirah wasn’t calling just to razz his younger brother. He was trying to squeeze a gameplan clue or two out of him.

“But he wasn’t really trying to tell me anything,” Jirah laughed.

When WSU and Fresno State kick off on Saturday evening, it won’t just mark the beginning of Pac-12 play for the Cougars and Bulldogs. It will also pit Jirah and Jonah against each other for the first time , a seminal moment in their lives, a full-circle moment for their parents and the ones who know them best.

The dynamics are interesting. Jirah has started three of the Cougars’ first four games of the season, becoming a cornerstone on the interior of his team’s defensive line. That would set him up to line up right across from Jonah, who started the Bulldogs’ season opener at right guard – except there’s one problem. Jonah, listed as questionable on the first Pac-12 availability report, isn’t expected to be able to play.

After playing 15 snaps in Fresno State’s season-opening loss to USC last month, Jonah went down with an injury. He wasn’t cleared to play in time for Saturday’s game in Pullman, according to his father, Tony, who called the experience exciting for the family since Jonah will still be at the game. Parents Tony and Rhonda will still be in attendance with their other five children, all the way from Apple Valley, California, which sits about 100 miles outside Los Angeles.

Only those aren’t the only Leaupepeteles who will be in attendance at Gesa Field on Saturday. The list also includes an assortment of grandparents and nephews and nieces, Tony said. “They better be wearing 98 in crimson and gray,” Jirah said with a smile. Zoom out and you start to understand what this means to the Leaupepeteles.

“It is surreal. It hasn’t really hit us,” Tony said. “It’s a proud moment for me and my wife, and our kids that look up to their siblings, their older siblings. … When this schedule came out, we were like, ‘Oh, we have to come to this game. This is a game we must come to.’ ”

“I’m just very proud to see them live out their dreams and goals right now,” Rhonda added. “It’s exciting to hear all the smack talking. We tell them like, ‘Hey, you guys are brothers still.’ But it’s all fun and games.”

The Leaupepetele’s have certainly earned the opportunity, even if Jonah can’t play in Saturday’s game. After spending the first three years of his career at FCS Eastern Washington, where he totaled 24 tackles (five solo) and one for loss, Jirah transferred to WSU, where he’s done nothing short of prosper. In WSU’s loss to Arizona last weekend, Jirah tallied his first sack as a Cougar, giving him eight tackles on the year.

He’s also earned three quarterback pressures this fall, according to Pro Football Focus, underscoring the space that he takes up with his 6-foot-3, 349-pound frame. Jirah has become a key cog in defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit, registering 133 snaps in his first four games at WSU.

For his part, Jonah redshirted last year, his true freshman season at Fresno State. In short order, this season he earned the Bulldogs’ starting right guard job, jogging out for Fresno State’s first snaps of the season in Week 1.

He may not be able to line up against his older brother on Saturday evening, but the moment still means something to the family, to the brothers who shared a bedroom growing up.

“That’s my best friend right there,” Jirah said. “I love him to death, but we’re still on that field. He’s across the line. He’s wearing a different color of jersey. That’s the type of timing this is.”

Turns out, Jirah and Jonah were opposites as they grew up, their parents said. They may have shared a room growing up, but that was about as similar as they got in those days. Jirah is more strong-willed, his dad said, remembering times when Jirah made a decision and pursued it full-strength. Jonah is more reserved, Rhonda said, taking time to weigh all his options when mulling a decision.

Jirah is more into video games, while Jonah likes board games and puzzles. Back home in Apple Valley, there would be plenty of times when Jirah would stay up late playing video games, hooting and hollering at the screen. Then would come Jonah’s voice: “Bro, I’m trying to sleep.”

They aren’t huge trash-talkers in general, their parents say, only to each other. They had lots of opportunities over the years, sharing the field in different capacities, from youth football all the way to the high school state championships. Jirah’s favorite memory of playing with Jonah, he said, was when they helped take Apple Valley to the CIF in Jonah’s freshman year, Jirah’s junior season.

“That was kinda really his first year taking football seriously, and that’s when he decided it was something that he really wanted to do,” Jirah said. “Just seeing him grow into the player that he is, and the person that he has become now is just really great to see.”

So the brothers may not square off directly across from each other when Saturday night arrives, but they’ll be in the same stadium, the same game as each other. That means something to them. It also means something special to Tony and Rhonda, the ones who raised them, and the family members that helped make the boys’ journey possible.

“After, they’ll smack talk and then they’ll look back on it,” Tony said. “They’re excited just living in the moment as far as preparing with their team, and then talking about, man, my brother’s literally on the opposite side of the field, and I’m on this side of the field, and this is gonna be the first time that we’ll go against each other. Obviously, Jonah, he’s not gonna be playing, but it’s gonna mean something for them – a win or a loss.”

Washington State.title: WSU, UW cover as the rebuilt Pac-12 opens conference play | Week 5 picks
Washington State.summary:
Welcome to the Hotline’s weekly picks against the point spread, published Thursdays throughout the regular season with a focus on the most intriguing matchups across the West and the top games nationally. Betting lines are courtesy of VegasInsider.com unless noted otherwise. (Games involving FCS teams not included.) I went 10-3-1 last week and am 25-23-2 for the season. Picks are for entertainment purposes only … unless they aren’t.

If the adage is true – that good coaches win but great coaches cover – the rebuilt Pac-12 has several future Hall of Famers on its payroll.

The first month of the first season of the conference’s return to competition produced a 19-12-1 record against the point spread, according to TeamRankings.com, the wagering and analytics website.

But that mark includes a pair of .500 teams (Texas State and Utah State) and one complete flop: San Diego State’s struggles on the field (1-3) are exceeded only by the Aztecs’ 0-4 performance against the spread.

The other five teams are crushing the point spread as conference play begins this weekend.

Oregon State and first-year coach JaMarcus Shephard have covered in all four games – the betting public has not recognized OSU’s improvement – while Boise State, Fresno State and Washington State are all 3-1 and Colorado State is 2-1-1.

Those five teams are a combined 15-4-1.

The success is undoubtedly appreciated in some corners, but it won’t help the conference when the College Football Playoff selection committee determines which Group of Six team will receive the automatic bid.

That calculation will lean into the wins and losses of the teams involved in the race, in addition to a handful of performance metrics connected to the strength of the conference overall.

In that respect, the Pac-12 compares reasonably well to its primary competition.

It posted a 9-4 record against the other Group of Six leagues, including a 3-2 mark against the American and 3-0 against the Mountain West. And it stands as the highest-ranked Group of Six conference in the Sagarin computer ratings.

All of which means a Pac-12 champion with no more than two losses should be well positioned for a CFP bid.

To the picks …

Stanford (+131/2

) at Wake Forest

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ACC Network

Comment: We picked the Cardinal last week to beat Georgia Tech outright (cha-CHING!) but do not like this situation one bit. The long trip, early kickoff, quality opponent and likelihood of rain add up to an easy call. Pick: Wake Forest

Michigan (-51/2

) at Minnesota

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on Fox

Comment: Based on how the teams fared last week, with Michigan losing at home to Iowa and Minnesota winning at Washington, the spread seems a tad high. But the Hotline won’t fall prey to recency bias. We expect the Wolverines to pull away late for the victory. Pick: Michigan

Cal (+21/2

) at UNLV

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network

Comment: The resistible force (Cal’s offense) meets the movable object (UNLV’s defense) in what could be a highly entertaining, although not well played, affair in Sin City. Both teams are desperate after splitting their first four games, but the Bears have better personnel. Pick: Cal

UTEP (+221/2

) at New Mexico

Kickoff: 1 p.m. on MW+

Comment: The Lobos are 4-0 against the point spread and have covered by an average of 161/2 points, according to TeamRankings.com. The trend is our friend. Pick: New Mexico

Oregon State (-61/2

) at Colorado State

Kickoff: 3 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: Perhaps the most interesting game of the opening week of conference play in the new Pac-12. If the Beavers truly belong on the top tier with Boise State, they will handle the defensively challenged Rams without much difficulty. For the moment, that’s exactly how we see it. Pick: Oregon State

BYU (-61/2

) at TCU

Kickoff: 4 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Cougars had two weeks to prepare while the Horned Frogs were losing last weekend at UCF. Frankly, we’re surprised the spread isn’t closer to double digits. Bear Bachmeier should have his way with TCU’s pass defense. Pick: BYU

Washington (+91/2

) at USC

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on NBC

Comment: Both teams are reeling, but we suspect the Trojans will have more difficulty recovering emotionally from yet another loss to Oregon. Also, this is strength on strength with USC’s offense matched against UW’s defense and vice versa. That suggests a close game throughout. Pick: Washington

Utah State (+20) at Boise State

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network

Comment: This feels like a letdown situation for the Broncos after their big win at Western Michigan. The Aggies don’t have enough offense to produce an upset, but they should hang around just long enough to cover that rather large number. Pick: Utah State

Fresno State (+2) at Washington State

Kickoff: 6:30 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: This is tantamount to a must-win game for WSU (1-3) in order to make the bowl math work. Meanwhile, the Bulldogs have started slowly in a handful of games and can’t afford to fall too far behind. The points are enticing, but the Cougars played well enough against Arizona to make us lean toward the home side. Pick: Washington State

Baylor (+4) at Arizona State

Kickoff: 7:30 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Sun Devils are home for the first time since the season opener, having lost at Texas A&M, beaten Kansas in London, then taken a week off to recover. As a result of the disruption, we expect a sluggish start and strong finish against an opponent that isn’t good enough to take full advantage of its chances. Pick: Arizona State

Texas State (-7) at San Diego State

Kickoff: 7:30 p.m. on The CW

Comment: The visitors opened as 41/2-point favorites, prompting a money flow strong enough to push the line to 7. And if that doesn’t frame the state of affairs for SDSU, nothing does. However, the Hotline will take the opportunity to zag while everyone else zigs. Pick: San Diego State

Cincinnati (+61/2

) at Arizona

Kickoff: 8 p.m. on Fox

Comment: The Bearcats are 4-0 but have yet to play a road game while the Wildcats are 3-1 with the loss coming on the road to a ranked opponent (BYU). Cincinnati has one of the best ground games in the country (270 yards per game). Arizona’s trouble against the run in Provo suggests a supreme challenge Saturday night – and the need for some fourth-quarter Noah Fifita heroics. Pick: Cincinnati

Straight-up winners: Wake Forest, Michigan, Cal, New Mexico, Oregon State, BYU, USC, Boise State, Washington State, Arizona State, San Diego State and Arizona.

Five-star special: BYU. Nothing TCU has done thus far, particularly the loss to North Carolina, indicates the Horned Frogs can match the Cougars yard for yard and score for score for four quarters.

Washington State.title: What's behind some of the WSU defense's struggles? Check out some of their snap counts
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – A few minutes after halftime began and Washington State players filed into their locker room, the sparkly new crimson and black lair that was remodeled over the summer, linebacker Keith Brown turned to a teammate with a question.

“What’s the score?” asked the sixth-year linebacker.

It was Saturday evening, and WSU had just taken a three-point lead on visiting Arizona into halftime, but Brown was none the wiser, according to his retelling. Brown and the Cougars’ defense had yielded a pair of scoring drives, and because quarterback Caden Pinnick had thrown an interception, that unit had to be on the field for one extra drive.

As the rest of the game unfolded, the Cougs lost one more turnover, a fumble from Pinnick on a play where he was trying to throw the ball away as he was getting tackled. That was the seventh turnover WSU’s offense has committed this season, which has spawned all kinds of other problems, perhaps this above all: The Cougars’ defense has been tasked with playing tons more snaps, lots more drives, putting them at risk of tiring themselves out when they shouldn’t have to.

For his part, Brown says it isn’t much of a problem.

“I don’t even think about it, man,” Brown said. “As a defender, you’re so excited to go out there and play, no matter what. … We just go out there every single series, and that series right there is the only thing I’m worried about. I don’t care if I just came off the field or the offense has been out there for a while. I’m excited to go out there and play.”

That may be the case, but it also means WSU defenders are playing heavy amounts of snaps. Check out some of the total snap counts from the Cougars’ loss to the Wildcats last weekend. Cornerback Khamari Terrell led all defenders with 72 snaps. Then came Brown, who logged 69, followed by defensive backs Jackquintin Bal with 67 and Jamarey Smith with 61.

That was the second time at least three WSU defenders played at least 60 snaps each, joining the team’s earlier loss to Kansas State: defensive backs Kai Rapolla, Jaylen Thomas and Smith all cleared the 60-snap mark.

Headed into WSU’s next game, a home matchup with Fresno State to kick off Pac-12 play, two defenders have hit the 200-snap threshold: Thomas leads the team with 225 snaps while Brown is on his heels with 222. Several others are in the area, including Smith at 199, linebacker DJ Warner at 196 and safety Jeremiah Bernard at 192.

Does that add up over time? Or does it all come out in the wash for a bunch of 19- to 22-year-olds?

“It adds up in fact that you’re going against a really good quarterback,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said, referring to Arizona’s Noah Fifita, “and we were very aggressive on defense, and you saw that in the first half. Over time, he’s gonna make some plays. He’s gonna create some passes downfield, and they had the quick drive right there, and just keeping our guys fresh because the coverage and the front, it’s all gotta work together. If the front is tired and we’re not getting the rush that we want to, well, that’s affecting the back end. That’s what we gotta get solved there in the third quarter, and it really starts playing complementary football.”

Perhaps no single stat illustrates the point better than this: WSU’s defense ranks in the top half of the country in points allowed in the first quarter, permitting just 4.3, which ranks No. 57 nationally. In the fourth quarter, the Cougars are allowing an average of 11.3 points, which ranks No. 123 nationally, only about a dozen spots up from last in the country.

Think about the way WSU’s defense was operating in the first quarter against Arizona. Defensive end Linus Zunk earned a sack on the first play of the game. Bal snagged that pick-six. Then later in the first quarter, defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepele got home for another sack. “Just doing my job,” he said about that play.

The Cougs (1-3) couldn’t replicate that level of production in the second half. The Wildcats won the second half to the tune of 20-7, averaging nearly 7 yards per play, keeping Fifita clean the rest of the game.

In other words, WSU defenders wore down as the game unfolded, which is partially to be expected of a group headed out onto the field so often. The Cougars have lost seven turnovers on the season, remember? Only 18 other teams in the country have committed more. That sets up defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit with more and more series, and while the Cougars could certainly be doing more on defense – their inability to get much pressure on Fifita in Saturday’s second half loomed large, as did a long touchdown rush K-State broke off earlier this month – check out their high snap counts and you start to understand the root of the issue.

So what’s the solution? Play more defenders? That isn’t feasible in all of WSU’s position groups. Cornerback Jalil Tucker, a starter in Week 1, has missed the last three games with an injury. Linebacker Nylan Brown was out last week. Defensive ends Malachi Wrice and Mike Hughes were too, and they figure to be out this Saturday against Fresno State. The Cougars could get more out of young safety Kyle Peterson, for example, but after he made an early mistake that led to an Arizona touchdown, he didn’t see the field again.

What about other players on the roster? Could the Cougs give more looks to guys like defensive lineman Josh Wedel (73 snaps) or defensive end Ben Beatty, who has played just 67 snaps? The latter seems possible, but in an interesting development, WSU coaches have never separated starters Zunk and Matyus McLain. They have both played 184 snaps, indicating that coaches like them best when they’re on the field together.

With that in mind, it’s possible that the best respite for this WSU defense is an improved offense, an offense that can sustain drives. The Cougars figure to have an easier time doing that against the likes of Fresno State than they did against Power Four foes like Washington, Kansas State and Arizona. If they can hold onto the ball against the Bulldogs – whose defense ranks sixth nationally with a plus-seven turnover margin – the Cougs won’t just be doing their offense a favor.

They’ll also be doing a favor to their defense.

Washington State.title: WSU men's hoops releases full 2026-27 schedule
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State’s first men’s basketball schedule in the rebuilt Pac-12 has arrived.

In coach David Riley’s third season, the Cougars have five home nonconference games in Pullman, and their Pac-12 opener is set for Jan. 3 at Fresno State. WSU will also play 11 nonconference games away from Pullman, the program’s most since 1973-74, underscoring the ways coaches have to keep budgets in mind when building schedules in this new athletics ecosystem.

WSU has a home game on Nov. 14 against Kirkland, of the NAIA ranks, marking the Cougars’ first time hosting a non-Division-I opponent since 2015.

WSU and Gonzaga will meet in Pullman on Jan. 6, which is a Wednesday during the Cougars’ winter break, and in Spokane on Feb. 17.

In the new Pac-12, it’s become clear that teams will play primarily on Wednesdays and Saturdays, which is the case for the majority of the Cougars’ games. They have a few games set for Sunday, particularly early in the conference slate, but those will be the most prevalent game days.

It’s also now official that for the first time since 1917, WSU and rival Washington will not play a regular-season game against each other. Instead, the clubs will meet for an exhibition matchup Oct. 25 in Seattle.

The beginning of the new Pac-12 schedule won’t be easy for WSU, which faces a stretch of three of four road games: at Boise State, at home against San Diego State, then on the road to face Colorado State and Utah State, the last of which figures to be a new conference power.

The Cougars also have what figures to be a brutal two-game stretch Feb. 17 and Feb. 20, which include road games against Gonzaga and San Diego State, respectively.

The new Pac-12 Tournament is set for March 9–13 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas.

Washington State.title: WSU set to host Fresno State to kick off competition in rebuilt Pac-12 | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here ’s a first look at Washington State’s home game against Fresno State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

To kick off competition in the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU hosts Fresno State, looking to turn around a 1-3 start to the season. In the teams’ first meeting in Pullman since 1994, WSU coach Kirby Moore squares off against the program that gave him his first FBS coaching gig – he worked as the Bulldogs’ receivers coach/offensive coordinator from 2017-22.

In the Cougars’ third straight home game, it’s possible that tight end Trey Leckner makes his season debut after missing the season’s first four games with a foot injury.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 6:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around a 21/2-point favorite in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 34-24 loss to Arizona, WSU took an early lead thanks to one touchdown from QB Caden Pinnick and a pick-six from safety Jackquintin Bal, but Arizona wasted no time leveling the game and won the second half, 20-7. The Cougars drew within one score late on a long touchdown pass from Pinnick to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, but that’s as close as they came, falling to 1-3 to open Moore’s debut season.

Pinnick completed 24 of 41 passes for 241 yards, two total touchdowns and two turnovers, one interception and one fumble. He’s now lost five turnovers this season, and the Cougars are up to seven as a whole, good for a total turnover margin of minus-4, which is tied for No. 119 nationally. It’s been a key reason behind some of the struggles of offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s group.

The Cougars played an OK game on defense, but they couldn’t slow down Wildcat QB Noah Fifita, who went 22-for-36 passing for 297 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. WSU also couldn’t limit receiver Tre Spivey, who hauled in seven catches for 129 yards and two touchdowns.

Four Cougar defenders played at least 60 snaps, led by cornerback Khamari Terrell with 72, perhaps opening a window into some of the reasons why WSU’s defense wore down in that game: Its best players were on the field too long.

“It adds up in fact that you’re going against a really good quarterback,” Moore said, “and we were very aggressive on defense, and you saw that in the first half. Over time, he’s gonna make some plays. He’s gonna create some passes downfield, and they had the quick drive right there, and just keeping our guys fresh because the coverage and the front, and it’s all gotta work together. If the front is tired and we’re not getting the rush that we want to, well, that’s affecting the back end. That’s what we gotta get solved there in the third quarter, and it really starts playing complementary football.”

In the third quarter, WSU slogged through some listless football, putting up several forgettable numbers: zero points, 149 total yards, 44 rushing yards, two three-and-outs, four punts and three sacks taken, giving Pinnick 10 sacks taken on the season. That opened the door for Arizona to turn a three-point deficit into a four-point lead, cushioning two more scoring drives in the fourth frame.

In the end, it added up to more question marks for WSU’s offense (two turnovers) and its special teams units, which had one field goal blocked and gave up a 39-yard punt return. The Cougars have now had two field goals blocked and given up two long punt returns, including a 62-yarder against Kansas State in Week 2.

The only bright spot on WSU’s special teams group has been punter Max Dean, who battled migraines in Saturday’s game to record five punts for 200 total yards, an average of 40 yards. He’s now averaging 45.2 yards per punt, which ranks No. 14 in the country.

Scouting Fresno State …

The Bulldogs, off to a 3-1 start to the season, are led by second-year head coach Matt Entz and quarterback Jayden Mandal. They began the year with a 39-0 road loss to USC before bouncing back with three straight wins: 49-3 over Sacramento State, 26-10 over San Jose State and 38-24 over Rice, the last of which unfolded last weekend.

Fresno State, which ranks No. 6 in the country with a turnover margin of plus-7, have the Pac-12’s best defense so far. The Bulldogs are allowing just 19 points per game, which ranks at the top in the conference, and star cornerback Simeon Harris has already collected three interceptions. As a team, Fresno State has also recovered three fumbles, tied for the conference lead.

The Bulldogs have also registered nine sacks, second in the conference, including two from linebacker Titus Khajavi and one apiece from six different players. Their Pro Football Focus pass rush grade of 65.3 ranks third in the Pac-12.

“That’s gonna be really important,” Moore said, “to make sure we take care of the football.”

On offense, Mandal has completed 67 of 104 passes (64%) for 789 yards, six touchdowns and one interception. His top target has been senior receiver Josiah Freeman – who was in his true freshman redshirt season in 2022, Moore’s final year at Fresno State – has totaled 18 catches for 261 yards and two touchdowns.

“The receiver was there when I was there. He was a really good, athletic player,” Moore said. “You see him show up on third downs and a lot of different situations.”

But a lot of the Bulldogs’ offense has also come from veteran running back Rayshon Luke, the Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Week. In Fresno State’s win over Rice, he tallied a game and career-high 167 yards with one touchdown on just 11 carries, giving him 240 rushing yards total on the season. He’s also averaging 6.7 yards per carry, which ranks third in the Pac-12.

What happened last time?

WSU and Fresno State’s last meeting came in 2024, when the Cougars eked out a 25-17 road win in Fresno. The Cougars got a key pick-six in the fourth quarter from cornerback Ethan O’Connor, who went on to transfer to Miami over the offseason.

Washington State.title: WSU TE Trey Leckner to be gametime decision against Fresno State, plus other injury updates and notes
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State tight end Trey Leckner is on track to return earlier than anybody quite expected.

That’s the word from coach Kirby Moore, who said Monday that Leckner will be a game-time decision Saturday evening against Fresno State, adding that he “will be back full -go this week in practice.”

A likely starter if he were healthy, Leckner suffered a foot injury over the summer. At the beginning of the season, Moore said Leckner was expected to miss the first half of the season, which would have put his return a few more weeks away. But it appears Leckner has made quicker progress than anticipated.

Whenever he returns, Leckner figures to provide a nice boost to the Cougars’ offense, which is still finding its footing amid the team’s 1-3 start to the season. Leckner is the team’s best pass-catching tight end, which could help unlock a WSU offense that has lost seven total turnovers.

In Leckner’s absence, WSU’s starting tight end has been UCLA transfer Jack Pedersen, who has caught five passes for 20 yards and one touchdown, which came against FCS Duquesne.

“We wanna be able to utilize both those guys. Obviously, try and get our best players on the field on offense,” Moore said. “That’ll probably be determined how (Leckner) looks today, Tuesday, Wednesday with the big work days. But I think he’s really progressed from the previous week, last week, and so he’s definitely shown that in the past, and we’re excited to get him out there.”

A redshirt junior from Snohomish, Leckner started nine of 13 games last season, catching 24 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns, which tied for the third-most by a tight end in WSU single-season history. In 2024, he played in 12 games (two as a starter), reeling in three passes for 56 yards and one score.

Tucker remains questionable

Starting cornerback Jalil Tucker remains “game-to-game, day-to-day,” Moore said. Tucker has now missed three straight games after sustaining an injury in the Sept. 6 Apple Cup. A transfer from Oregon State, Tucker dressed and warmed up for each of the Cougars’ past two games, but he hasn’t been able to play.

In Tucker’s absence, WSU has tried a couple different approaches. Against Kansas State, the Cougars went with redshirt senior Kai Rapolla, who had a forgettable game, missing two tackles and allowing three catches on four targets. Against Duquesne and Arizona, they moved nickelback Jamarey Smith to cornerback and brought safety Jackquintin Bal off the bench, the latter of which turned out to be a great decision from WSU – Bal returned an interception 25 yards for a touchdown.

If Tucker can’t play Saturday against Fresno State, look for coaches to go with the same approach. They might even give more snaps to Bal, who played a career-high 67 snaps last weekend against Arizona, earning an expanded role in defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit. He also recorded nine tackles against Arizona, tops on the team and also Bal’s career-best.

“Just doing my 1/11th, trying to be myself and just try to be the best person I can be in my position,” Bal said after the Arizona game, “no matter if it’s boundary safety, field safety, just doing my part.”

Extra points• Moore seemed to stand by his decision to let 40 seconds tick off the clock at the end of Saturday’s first half against Arizona, when the Cougars had first-and-10 from the Wildcats’ 12-yard line. WSU got a field goal, but Moore explained that he didn’t want to give the ball back to Arizona QB Noah Fifita and his explosive offense.

“Whether we scored or we kicked a field goal too early, giving the ball back to that quarterback,” Moore said, “I did not think was in our best interest before the half.”

• How can the Cougars generate more explosive plays, which Moore has often expressed a need for, when those are the times QB Caden Pinnick has lost turnovers? Moore said this: “It’s definitely a balance. It’s dialogue during the week. If something’s there, if it’s not there, self-preservation, making sure we’re playing the next play. Every play has a life of its own, and we had some of that come up on Saturday.”

Washington State.title: THE PALOUSE REPORT: First Week of College Football! WE ARE BACK!
Washington State.summary:
Welcome to the FIRST EVER episode of THE PALOUSE PULSE, your new weekly college football roundup from the perspective of Washington State and WSU Football fans! 🔴⚪

College football is BACK, and Week Zero gave us plenty to talk about. We break down the biggest games from around the country and, more importantly, look at what they could mean for Washington State, the Pac-12, and the future of college football.

We dive into USC vs. San Jose State, North Carolina vs. TCU in Ireland, Virginia's impressive performance against NC State, North Dakota State's dominant FBS debut, Sacramento State's transition to FBS football, Florida State vs. New Mexico State, Stanford vs. Hawaii, and the wild Memphis vs. UNLV matchup.

But there's a bigger question behind all of it:

Could teams like North Dakota State, Montana State, Montana and South Dakota State eventually become major players in the Pac-12? 👀

With Washington State closely connected to the future of the Pac-12, these games and conference developments matter. We're going to be tracking them every week and breaking down the teams, players, games, and storylines that could eventually impact WSU Football.
